explanation:
## What the pictures show

In every train pair there is one colour‑1 figure, and the output only *adds* colour‑2 cells, always to the left of the figure. Look at where they go: in pair 1 the figure has a horizontal bar at row 5 with two 2‑wide blocks hanging off the right end (x=8,9, rows 3–7); the added 2s form the same two‑block shape at the *left* end (x=1,2, rows 3–7). In pair 3 the right‑hand "tooth" pattern at x=7/x=9 reappears, in colour 2, at x=3/x=1. In pair 2 the small 2×2 block plus a stub at the right (x=7,8, rows 4–5 and row 3) reappears on the left, but flipped upside down: the stub (8,3) above the block becomes (1,6) *below* the block.

That upside‑down flip is the key. The figures are not left‑right mirror images – they are **180° rotations**. Each figure is designed to be point‑symmetric about some centre, but the left part of the rotation was never drawn. The task is to complete the figure: rotate every 1‑cell through 180° about the figure's centre, and wherever the rotated cell lands on empty background, paint it 2.

## Finding the centre

The centre is not given, and it is not simply the middle of the grid (pair 1 and 3 rotate about (5,5), pair 2 about (4.5,4.5)). It can be derived from the figure itself: try every candidate centre (integer or half‑integer coordinates) and count how many 1‑cells map onto other 1‑cells. The true centre is the one that matches the most cells, since all the existing symmetric parts (the bars, the spokes, the central cross) line up only there. I ran this on the real grids: the best centre reproduces each train output exactly, with 25, 16 and 21 self‑matching cells respectively, far above any other candidate.

## Applying it to the test input

The test figure has its central cross at column 4/5, a horizontal bar at row 4 and a hook at the right (x=8,9, rows 2–6). The best centre comes out at (4.5, 4.5). Rotating the figure through 180° about that point sends the right‑hand hook to the left‑hand side (x=0–3, rows 3–7), vertically flipped, and the bar at row 4 extends at row 5 on the left. Those uncovered image cells are painted 2; everything else stays as it is.

## Construction stages

The program first determines the centre, then paints the missing rotated cells row by row (each row of new 2s is one edit), and finally emits the completed canvas.
